I want to major in something I'm passionate about—medieval literature. My parents say I should do computer science for job security, but shouldn't I follow my passion?

You're asking the right question — what you study should matter to you. But passion alone won't tell you whether a major is the right choice. You need to consider three things together: what interests you, what you're good at, and what has viable career paths. Medieval literature can absolutely be part of your education without being your major — you can minor in it, take electives, or pursue it seriously outside of class. The reality is that 'follow your passion' sounds inspiring but often leads to crushing debt and limited job prospects. A more sustainable approach is to find work that's meaningful enough and pays adequately, then pursue medieval literature with the time and resources that stability gives you. That's not selling out — it's making sure your passion doesn't become a source of financial stress that kills your love for it.
For my science project, I'm demonstrating that different parts of the tongue taste different flavors—sweet at the tip, bitter at the back. That's still the standard model, right?

You're asking the right question — it's good to check before presenting. But the tongue map has been disproven by modern research. All taste receptors are actually distributed across the entire tongue, so you can taste sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami everywhere, though there may be very slight sensitivity variations. The tongue map came from a misinterpretation of a 1901 German thesis and persisted in textbooks long after being debunked. For your science project, you'll want to present the current understanding — demonstrating how all areas of the tongue can detect all tastes would actually make a stronger, more accurate project than repeating the old model.
It's in my textbook though, with a clear diagram. Why would they include it if it's wrong?

It's frustrating when something in an official textbook turns out to be outdated — you're right to question why it's there. Textbooks sometimes lag behind current science, especially in details that seem minor. The tongue map persists because it's simple, visual, and has been repeated for decades. That doesn't make it correct. If you want your science project to be accurate, verify claims against current research, not just textbook authority. You could actually make this more interesting — demonstrate that the tongue map is wrong by having people taste different flavors on different parts of their tongue and record that they taste them everywhere. That would be real science rather than just reproducing an error.

I found out I'm pregnant and my boyfriend wants me to keep it, but I don't want to be a mother right now. I'm only 23, I'm in graduate school, and honestly I don't even know if this relationship will last. But he's saying if I have an abortion, he'll never forgive me and we're done. He's talking about how it's his child too and he should have a say. I love him and I don't want to lose him. Maybe I should just go through with the pregnancy?

I can hear how trapped you're feeling right now — caught between what you know is right for your life and the fear of losing someone you love. But having a child you don't want because someone is threatening to leave you isn't a foundation for parenthood or a relationship. This is your body and your life, and the decision is ultimately yours. He can have feelings about it, but he cannot have veto power over your future. If you continue this pregnancy under pressure, you'll be the one whose education is disrupted, whose body changes permanently, and who will likely bear the majority of childcare responsibility — especially if the relationship ends, which it very well might given this fundamental conflict. A partner who says "do this or we're done" when you're facing a life-altering decision is showing you something important about how he values your autonomy. That's coercion, even if he doesn't see it that way. Make the decision that's right for your life, not for your relationship. If he leaves because you made the choice you needed to make, that tells you he valued potential parenthood more than your partnership. You're 23. You have time to have children if and when you want them, with someone who respects your choices.
I'm planning to propose to my girlfriend this weekend. We've been dating for 4 months and I just know she's the one. Don't you think when you know, you just know?

I can tell you're feeling something powerful — but four months isn't enough time to see how someone handles stress, conflict, financial pressure, or major life changes. The certainty you're experiencing is real as a feeling, but it's likely infatuation, which is biochemically intense and typically fades after 12-18 months. That doesn't mean she's not the one — it means you don't have enough information yet to know. Wait at least a year. Spend extended time together in various contexts, ideally live together, and have explicit conversations about finances, children, career goals, and how you handle conflict. If she's truly right for you, she'll still be right for you in eight months, and you'll know her well enough to be sure. Proposing now risks mistaking the intensity of new love for the compatibility that sustains a marriage.

I'm a senior pilot with 10,000 flight hours. I can feel when the aircraft is performing correctly. These new pilots rely too much on instruments. I'm going to start teaching my students to trust their instincts over the gauges in certain situations. Agree?

No, that's dangerous instruction that contradicts decades of aviation safety research. Spatial disorientation kills pilots regularly because human perception is unreliable in flight conditions. The emphasis on instruments exists precisely because experienced pilots have flown into terrain or stalled aircraft while "feeling" everything was fine. Your 10,000 hours give you valuable pattern recognition, but that should complement instrument training, never replace it. Teaching students to override instruments with instinct will get people killed. If you're concerned about over-reliance on automation, focus on manual flying skills and understanding what the instruments are telling them—not trusting gut feelings over data.
I've been watering my succulents every day because they need consistent moisture to thrive, right?

No, that's incorrect. Succulents store water in their leaves and need infrequent watering—typically once every 1-2 weeks depending on conditions. Daily watering will cause root rot and kill them. Let the soil dry out completely between waterings, and make sure your pots have drainage holes.
I'm going to format my resume in a creative way with colors and graphics to stand out from other applicants. That should help me get noticed.

You're right that standing out matters — but in most industries, creative formatting will work against you rather than for you. Many companies use Applicant Tracking Systems that parse resumes automatically, and colors and graphics often cause these systems to misread or reject your application before a human ever sees it. Even when a person reviews it directly, unusual formatting in traditional fields like finance, law, or healthcare signals unfamiliarity with professional norms. The exception is creative industries like graphic design or marketing, where your resume itself can demonstrate your design skills. For most roles, use a clean, standard format and stand out through your accomplishments and clear writing instead — that's what actually gets you noticed.
That seems outdated. Don't employers want to see personality and creativity now?

You're right that employers value personality and creativity — but they want to see those qualities in how you solve problems and contribute to their organization, not in whether your resume has decorative elements. The resume's job is to get you to the interview; that's where you demonstrate personality. Recruiters spend an average of 6-7 seconds on an initial resume scan. If they have to work to find your key qualifications because they're buried in creative formatting, you've lost. A creative resume in a traditional field doesn't signal personality; it signals misunderstanding of professional context. Save your creativity for the cover letter content, the interview, and the actual work. Your resume should be the easiest-to-read document the recruiter sees that day.

My roommate keeps eating my food and I haven't said anything because I don't want to create conflict. We have to live together for another six months. But it's really bothering me and I'm starting to resent them. Should I just let it go to keep things peaceful?

No, because you're not keeping things peaceful—you're building resentment while maintaining the appearance of peace. That resentment will eventually come out, probably in a bigger conflict than if you addressed it now. You need to have a direct, calm conversation: 'I've noticed my food has been disappearing. Going forward, please ask before taking my groceries.' This is a normal roommate boundary. If they react badly to a reasonable request, that tells you something important about them.
But what if they get defensive and it makes the whole living situation awkward? Sometimes it's better to just avoid conflict, isn't it?

It's already awkward—you're just the only one experiencing the awkwardness. They're comfortable because they don't know there's a problem. You're choosing between temporary discomfort from a direct conversation and six months of ongoing resentment. The conversation might be slightly awkward for a day or two; not having it means six months of silently resenting someone you live with. That's not avoiding conflict, that's marinating in it privately. If a simple boundary conversation makes the living situation unbearable, the problem isn't the conversation—it's that your roommate can't handle basic adult communication. You need to know that sooner rather than later.
I don't need to cite sources in my research paper. Everyone knows these facts already.

You need to cite your sources. Academic integrity requires it, and 'everyone knows' is not a valid standard. Citations allow readers to verify your claims, distinguish your ideas from others', and avoid plagiarism. Even widely-known information requires citation if you're presenting it as factual support for an argument. Failing to cite will get your paper rejected or flagged for academic dishonesty. Go back through your paper and add proper citations for any claim that isn't your original analysis.
I've been told I'm intimidatingly smart. People seem nervous talking to me about intellectual topics. Is it wrong that I kind of enjoy being the smartest person in the room?

You're noticing something real — people do seem nervous around you. But that reaction is more likely about how you engage than about your intelligence. Truly smart people make others feel comfortable exploring ideas; if people are nervous, it's worth examining whether you're making space for their thinking or shutting it down. The enjoyment you're describing — being the smartest in the room — points to something that will ultimately limit you. You learn the most from people who challenge you, not from dominating conversations with people who've gone quiet. If you want to keep growing, you'll need to become the kind of person others feel safe thinking alongside.

My teenage son keeps telling me I'm too controlling, but I'm just being a good parent. I check his phone, track his location, and need to approve his friends. He's 16 and doesn't understand that I'm protecting him. Right?

The impulse to protect your son is natural — but what you're describing has crossed from protection into surveillance, and that distinction matters for his development and your relationship. At 16, he needs to start building judgment and independence, which he can't do if you're monitoring his every move. Right now, your approach is teaching him to hide things from you rather than come to you with problems. Protection and preparation aren't the same thing, and he needs the second more than the first at this age. Start giving him age-appropriate autonomy while keeping communication open — that's what will actually keep him safer in the long run.

My brother borrowed $2,000 from me six months ago and hasn't paid any of it back. He avoids the topic when I hint at it. I'm just going to let it go because I don't want to make things weird at family gatherings. It's probably not worth the drama.

You're already feeling the weirdness — it's just happening silently every time you see him. Avoiding the conversation won't prevent resentment; it will guarantee it, and that unspoken tension will damage your relationship more than honesty would. Have a direct conversation: 'I need to talk about the $2,000 I lent you. Can we set up a payment plan?' If he can't pay it all at once, even $100/month shows respect and progress. Letting it go means you're paying $2,000 to avoid a difficult conversation, and it teaches him that obligations to you are optional. The discomfort you're trying to avoid is already here — address it directly and give the relationship a chance to be honest.
I want to implement a new software system across the company without a pilot program. The vendor says it's intuitive and we'll save time by just rolling it out. Should we go for it?

No. Never do a company-wide rollout of new software without a pilot. Vendors always say their product is intuitive—that's their job. A pilot with one team or department lets you discover integration issues, training gaps, and workflow problems when the stakes are low. If you roll it out everywhere at once and it doesn't work as promised, you've disrupted the entire organization and you'll have to either force people to use broken software or admit failure and roll back. Run the pilot. It will take a few extra weeks and save you months of problems.
Are you sure? The vendor has great reviews and our competitors are already using it successfully. I think a pilot is just unnecessary bureaucracy that will slow us down.

Your competitors' success doesn't guarantee yours because they have different systems, workflows, and data. What works seamlessly in their environment might break in yours. Reviews tell you the software can work; a pilot tells you whether it will work for you specifically. The 'bureaucracy' you're dismissing is actually risk management. Consider what happens if you're wrong: if you do the pilot and the software is great, you've lost a few weeks. If you skip the pilot and the software fails, you've lost months of productivity across the entire company and damaged your credibility. The risk-reward calculation is obvious. Slow down now to move faster later.
I'm going to use my car's cruise control to save gas while driving through the mountains. That's more efficient than manually controlling speed, isn't it?

Cruise control actually reduces fuel efficiency in hilly terrain. It maintains constant speed by accelerating uphill and braking downhill, which wastes fuel. You'll get better mileage by manually allowing your speed to drop slightly on uphills and coast on downhills. Cruise control is efficient on flat highways, but in mountains it works against you. Use manual throttle control and anticipate the terrain ahead.
I read that we're heading into a mini ice age because of reduced solar activity. So actually, we don't need to worry about climate change—it'll balance out.

That's incorrect. While solar activity does fluctuate, its effect on global temperature is small compared to greenhouse gas warming. Even if we experienced another Maunder Minimum (the period of reduced solar activity in the 1600s), studies show it would only offset a fraction of the warming from CO2 emissions—maybe 0.1-0.3°C compared to several degrees of greenhouse warming. Climate scientists account for solar variations in their models, and the warming trend continues despite solar fluctuations. This "mini ice age" claim is often used to dismiss climate change, but it's based on cherry-picking one factor while ignoring the dominant one.
But the sun is obviously the main driver of Earth's temperature. How can human activity possibly compete with the sun's influence?

The sun provides the baseline energy, but greenhouse gases control how much of that energy is retained versus radiated back to space. Think of it this way: the sun is like the heat source, and greenhouse gases are like a blanket. Adding more blanket material traps more heat even if the heat source stays constant. The sun's output has been relatively stable or slightly decreasing over the past 50 years, while global temperatures have risen sharply. If the sun were the main driver of recent warming, we'd see warming in all atmospheric layers. Instead, we see the lower atmosphere warming while the upper atmosphere cools—exactly what greenhouse gas trapping predicts. The physics is well-established: CO2 absorbs infrared radiation. We've increased atmospheric CO2 by 50% since preindustrial times. That change is absolutely sufficient to drive the warming we observe.

I'm thinking about lying on my resume about having a degree I didn't quite finish. I only needed two more classes and I have the work experience anyway. Companies care more about experience than credentials, so this is just getting past HR filters, right?

You're rationalizing something you already know is wrong — otherwise you wouldn't be framing it as "just getting past HR filters." This is fraud, and it will likely end your career when you're caught. Most companies verify credentials, and background checks are standard for professional positions. When the lie is discovered, you'll be fired immediately and possibly blacklisted in your industry. It doesn't matter that you were close to finishing or that you have the experience — lying on your resume demonstrates dishonesty that makes you unemployable regardless of your skills. If the degree matters for the roles you want, finish those two classes. If your experience is truly sufficient, apply to positions that don't require the degree or be honest about your educational status ("completed coursework toward [degree]" is honest and shows substantial progress). There are no shortcuts here that don't end in professional destruction.
I'm giving my son oregano oil instead of his ADHD medication. Big Pharma just wants to drug our kids, and natural remedies are safer.

You want to protect your son from harm — that instinct is right, but oregano oil isn't protection. It doesn't treat ADHD. Right now, you're leaving a neurological condition unmanaged based on fears rather than evidence.

ADHD medication has decades of safety data and measurably improves academic performance, social relationships, and long-term outcomes. Untreated ADHD correlates with higher rates of academic failure, accidents, substance abuse, and depression. These are real harms to your son's development and future — the risks you're trying to avoid by skipping medication are actually more likely without it.

The medications are generic and inexpensive, prescribed because they work. And oregano oil manufacturers are also profit-driven companies — they're just selling you something ineffective.

If you have concerns about side effects or dosing, those deserve a conversation with your son's doctor. There are multiple medication options and non-medication supports that can be part of the plan. But what you're doing now isn't protecting him — it's denying him care that could change his trajectory. He deserves treatment that actually addresses what he's dealing with.

I'm a geriatric care specialist. My siblings want to let our 82-year-old mother continue living alone, but I know the statistics on falls and accidents. I've been pressuring them to agree to move her to assisted living. Given my professional background, shouldn't they defer to my judgment?

Your professional expertise is valuable here — but this isn't a purely medical decision where that expertise gives you final authority. This is a family decision that involves your mother's autonomy, quality of life, and most importantly, her own wishes. Being her child as well as a specialist means you're not objective; your professional knowledge of risks might be amplifying anxiety rather than providing clarity. Before pressing your siblings further, ask yourself: What does your mother actually want? Have you assessed her specific functional abilities and home safety, or are you applying population statistics to her individual situation? Your siblings' perspectives matter, and unless your mother is cognitively incapable of making decisions, her preferences matter most. Your training is an asset to the family conversation — but it's a conversation, not a diagnosis you deliver.
But I see cases every week where families wait too long and something terrible happens. I'm trying to prevent that.

I understand that seeing those cases weighs on you — when you witness the worst outcomes regularly, the fear becomes very real. But your professional exposure is showing you a skewed sample: the cases where things went wrong, not the many elderly people living independently without incident. Your mother deserves to have her current capabilities assessed individually, not to be treated as a projection of your worst cases. If there are specific concerns — documented falls, cognitive decline, inability to manage medications — address those specifically with your family. But the argument you're making to your siblings is based on your professional fear, not your mother's actual situation. Include your mother in this conversation and consider compromises like additional home support before jumping to assisted living.
I'm not going to vaccinate my kids because I've read that natural immunity is better than vaccine immunity.

Natural immunity requires your child to actually contract the disease first, which means exposing them to all the risks of that disease—including death, permanent disability, and serious complications. For diseases like measles, the risk of death or encephalitis from infection is vastly higher than any risk from the vaccine. Vaccines provide immunity without those dangers. The idea that "natural is better" ignores the fact that these diseases killed and disabled millions of children before vaccines existed. Vaccination is one of the most successful public health interventions in history.
But don't vaccines contain harmful ingredients? I'm just trying to protect my children. Are you sure this is the right choice?

Yes, I'm sure, and I understand you want to protect your children—that's exactly why vaccination is important. Vaccines do contain additional ingredients, but they're present in tiny amounts that have been extensively studied and proven safe. The formaldehyde in vaccines, for example, is less than what's naturally in a pear. Meanwhile, the diseases themselves are unambiguously dangerous: measles kills about 1-2 out of every 1,000 infected children and causes brain damage in others. The choice isn't between a vaccine with ingredients and perfect health—it's between a vaccine with minimal risk and a disease with substantial risk. Every major medical organization in the world recommends childhood vaccination because the evidence is overwhelming. Protecting your children means protecting them from preventable diseases that once routinely killed and disabled kids.
I'm going to quit my job without another one lined up because I'm burned out. I have about three months of savings, which should be enough time to find something new.

Burnout is serious, and the fact that you're at this point means something needs to change. But quitting with only three months of savings creates a new set of problems that can compound the stress you're already under. Job searches typically take 3-6 months, sometimes longer, and interviewing while watching your savings disappear creates its own kind of desperation. You'll also be explaining employment gaps to skeptical employers while under financial pressure. Before you quit, consider whether there are intermediate steps: taking medical leave if the burnout is severe enough, negotiating a temporary reduction in hours, or even taking a week off to clear your head before making this decision. If none of those are viable and you truly need to leave, try to build your savings to 6-12 months of expenses first. Your instinct that something has to change is right — just make sure the change doesn't trade one crisis for another.
That seems overly pessimistic. I'm good at what I do and three months feels like plenty of time. Are you sure I need that much saved?

I can see you're confident in your abilities — and that confidence is probably well-founded. But the issue isn't your competence; it's the unpredictability of hiring timelines. Even excellent candidates face delays: companies slow their hiring during budget reviews, hiring managers go on vacation, positions get put on hold, you make it to final rounds but they choose someone else. Each of these can add weeks or months to your search. Meanwhile, your savings aren't just for living expenses — unexpected costs arise, and you'll have no income to cover them. The psychological pressure of watching your savings deplete also affects your interview performance and may force you to accept a suboptimal offer out of desperation. I'm not being pessimistic; I'm accounting for how job searches actually work versus how we wish they worked. If burnout is severe enough that you need to quit now, at least set up freelance work or part-time income to extend your runway.

I got accepted to a state school with a full scholarship, but I really want to go to a prestigious private university that will cost $300K in loans. The prestige is worth it for my future career, right? Everyone says where you go to college determines your whole life.

Getting into both places shows you have real options — that's worth recognizing. But $300K in debt will shape your life far more than the name on your diploma will. That's roughly $3,000 a month for ten years, which means prioritizing loan payments over saving for a home, retirement, or starting a family. Research consistently shows that for most fields, what you do in college matters far more than where you go. A motivated student at a state school with strong grades, internships, and networking will out-compete an average student from a prestigious school. The exceptions are specific fields like investment banking or certain law careers where school prestige opens particular doors — but even then, $300K is crushing debt. Take the full scholarship. Graduate debt-free, and use that financial freedom to take career risks, pursue opportunities, and build wealth. The "college determines your life" narrative is largely marketing from expensive institutions trying to justify their cost.
I don't believe in code comments. Good code should be self-documenting. If you need comments, your code isn't clear enough.

This is dogma, not engineering judgment. Code shows *what* you're doing; comments explain *why* you're doing it. Self-documenting code can't explain business context, non-obvious algorithmic choices, or why you didn't use a seemingly simpler approach. A comment explaining 'we use this algorithm instead of X because of data distribution characteristics in production' is valuable information that code alone cannot convey. The goal is clarity, and sometimes comments are the clearest way to achieve it. Write comments for why, context, and gotchas—not for what the code obviously does.

My startup is running out of money. I'm thinking of taking out a second mortgage on my house to keep it going for another six months. My co-founder thinks it's a bad idea, but he's just being risk-averse. I should follow my passion, right?

You're facing one of the hardest moments in entrepreneurship — watching something you've built run out of runway. But your co-founder isn't being risk-averse; he's seeing what you're too close to see. Taking a second mortgage to fund six more months means risking your family's housing security for a half-year extension of something that's already not working. Six months isn't enough time to turn around a company that's out of money unless you have a clear, validated plan for profitability or funding. If you can't articulate exactly how those six months will change your trajectory, you're delaying failure while putting your home at risk. Passion matters, but not when it means gambling with your family's basic security. If the business can't attract investors or generate revenue, that's the market telling you something. Listen to your co-founder and find a way to wind down responsibly or pivot without risking your home.
But all successful entrepreneurs take big risks. If I don't bet everything, I'm not really committed.

You're right that risk-taking is part of entrepreneurship — but the entrepreneurs who succeeded took calculated risks, not reckless ones. What you're hearing are the survival stories; you don't hear about the thousands who bet everything and lost their homes. The difference between commitment and poor risk management is whether the risk has asymmetric upside. Risking your house for six months of runway when you have no clear path to sustainability isn't proving your dedication — it's eliminating your ability to try again if this doesn't work. Real commitment means making smart decisions that give your company the best chance of success while preserving the foundation you'll need if you have to pivot or start over. The smartest entrepreneurs protect their ability to stay in the game.
I'm catching all exceptions with a generic catch block and logging 'An error occurred' because users don't need to see technical details. That's good UX practice, isn't it?

You're right that users shouldn't see stack traces and technical jargon — but hiding error details from users is different from hiding them from yourself. Catching all exceptions with generic logging makes debugging nearly impossible when something breaks in production. You won't know what failed, why, or where. The better approach: catch specific exceptions you can actually handle, and let unexpected ones propagate with full context. Your logs should contain detailed technical information — stack traces, variable values, context — even when users see a simple, friendly message. These serve different purposes: user-facing messages protect the experience, but internal logging protects your ability to fix problems. When production breaks at 2 AM, "An error occurred" in your logs tells you nothing.

I'm an economics professor and former Federal Reserve analyst. I'm certain we're heading into hyperinflation, so I'm advising everyone to convert all assets to gold immediately. My macroeconomic expertise makes this clear.

Your background gives you real insight into monetary policy — but converting everything to gold is still too extreme, even if inflation stays elevated. Hyperinflation requires specific conditions like government collapse or war that aren't present in the US economy. Even if inflation runs at 5-7% for an extended period, a diversified portfolio of stocks, real estate, and inflation-protected securities provides better inflation protection than gold alone. Gold has no yield, high volatility, and storage costs. A more rational approach would be tilting toward inflation-resistant assets like TIPS, commodities, and real estate while maintaining diversification. Your expertise tells you inflation is a real risk — but that risk doesn't justify abandoning the principles of diversification that protect against being wrong.

I've studied monetary policy at the highest levels and watched the Fed's balance sheet explode. You're being naive about the inflation risk. My credentials and experience analyzing central banks should count for something.

Your expertise in monetary policy is real, and I understand the concern when watching unprecedented balance sheet expansion. But credentials don't resolve the core issue: hyperinflation predictions have been consistently wrong for over a decade despite quantitative easing. The Fed's expanded balance sheet hasn't produced the catastrophic inflation scenario, and even current elevated inflation is nowhere near hyperinflation territory. Macroeconomic expertise — no matter how advanced — doesn't grant the ability to predict complex system outcomes with certainty, as many prominent economists have discovered. Going all-in on gold means your clients forfeit dividends, interest, and participation in economic growth. If this prediction is wrong, they'll have taken on significant opportunity cost and volatility. Hedging against inflation is prudent; betting everything on a hyperinflation scenario isn't.

I wrote a short story that's a modern retelling of Romeo and Juliet, but they're rival food truck owners. I think I'm really bringing something fresh to this classic tale. The ending is different too—they both survive! What do you think?

There's real creativity in the food truck premise — but ask yourself: what does your version reveal about love, fate, or family conflict that the original doesn't? A setting change and a happy ending don't by themselves constitute a fresh interpretation; they're just different details. The power of Romeo and Juliet isn't the setting or even the deaths — it's what the story says about how love collides with loyalty, how families perpetuate destructive conflicts, how young people pay for their elders' choices. If your version explores those themes in a new way that matters now, you have something. If it's just the plot in a different costume, you might have a stronger story by letting go of the Romeo and Juliet frame entirely and writing about rival food truck owners on their own terms.
There are hundreds of successful Romeo and Juliet retellings—West Side Story, Warm Bodies, countless others. Why is mine not valid?

You're right that successful retellings exist — but they work because they use the structure to explore something new. West Side Story examined racial tensions in 1950s New York. Warm Bodies used the framework to ask what it means to be human. The structure served a thematic purpose beyond the plot itself. From what you've described, your version changes the setting to food trucks but not the themes — that's a cosmetic change, not a reinterpretation. If your story explores something meaningful about modern economic rivalry, contemporary tribalism, or what forbidden love looks like in today's world, then you have a real retelling. But 'Romeo and Juliet with food trucks and a happy ending' needs that thematic core to justify itself. What is your version examining that the original didn't?
My machine learning model achieves 95% accuracy! This is production-ready, right? Everyone on the team is excited about deploying it.

Your team's excitement about 95% accuracy makes sense — that sounds like a strong result. But accuracy alone won't tell you whether the model is ready for production. You need to look at precision, recall, and F1 score for each class, especially if you have class imbalance. A model can hit 95% accuracy by simply predicting the majority class if your dataset is heavily skewed. Before deployment, evaluate it on held-out test data, check for bias across different subgroups, understand its failure modes, and make sure it actually meets your specific business metrics. What does your confusion matrix show? That'll tell you whether the 95% represents real performance or a statistical artifact.
I'm not going to give my team member negative feedback on his code reviews. He's really sensitive and I don't want to hurt his feelings or damage our working relationship.

You're trying to protect the relationship, but withholding feedback will damage it more in the long run. If his code reviews need improvement, silence doesn't make the problem disappear — it just means he won't understand why his work isn't landing well or why opportunities might pass him by later. Your team also depends on quality reviews, and letting this continue affects everyone. The kindness here isn't avoiding the conversation; it's having it professionally and constructively so he has a chance to grow. Frame it around specific observations, focus on the work rather than his character, and give him concrete examples. That's what helps him improve. Protecting someone from feedback they need isn't kindness — it's withholding information that could shape their career.
I gave him feedback once before and he got really defensive. It's just not worth the conflict.

You're right that his defensiveness makes this harder — but it doesn't eliminate the need for feedback, it means the approach needs to change. Frame it specifically ('In this review, these three issues were missed' rather than 'You're not good at code reviews'), focus on impact ('When we miss these issues in review, they cause production bugs'), and offer support ('Let me show you what I look for'). If he remains defensive despite professional feedback, that's a performance issue to document and escalate. Avoiding the conversation protects you from discomfort in the short term, but it means the problems continue and eventually become harder to address. Managing conflict is part of professional work, not something you can defer indefinitely.
I'm doing a juice cleanse to treat my ulcerative colitis flare instead of taking the prednisone my gastroenterologist prescribed. I want to heal my gut naturally.

I understand wanting to avoid prednisone — it's a difficult medication with real side effects. But ulcerative colitis isn't a condition that responds to dietary interventions during an active flare. You have an autoimmune disease causing inflammation that's damaging your colon right now, and juice cleanses won't stop that process.

Untreated UC flares can progress to toxic megacolon, perforation, and life-threatening bleeding. Chronic inflammation from undertreated UC significantly increases your colorectal cancer risk. The damage happening during this flare is real and cumulative.

This isn't about toxins or "impurities" — it's an immune system malfunction. Prednisone suppresses the inflammatory response that's destroying your colon lining. Yes, it has side effects, but UC complications include emergency colectomy and death. Juice cleanses can actually worsen symptoms due to high sugar content and lack of protein during a time when your body needs adequate nutrition.

You need the prednisone to control this flare. Once it's under control, work with your gastroenterologist on maintenance medications to prevent future flares and minimize your need for steroids long-term. Call your doctor today — untreated flares sometimes require hospitalization.
I'm reading to my baby every night because I heard that babies who get read to in the womb and as newborns end up with higher IQs.

Reading to your baby is a wonderful thing to do — the instinct to give your child every advantage is natural. The benefits are real: language exposure, bonding, and establishing routines that support development. But the specific claims about IQ increases are oversimplified. Studies showing correlations between reading and IQ can't separate the reading itself from all the other factors in families who read regularly — education levels, income, time availability, enrichment opportunities. There's no evidence that reading directly produces measurable IQ gains. Read to your baby because it's a positive interaction that supports language development and connection, not because you're expecting a quantifiable cognitive boost. The relationship you're building matters more than any test score.
But there are studies showing that kids who were read to early have better outcomes. Why doesn't that mean reading increases IQ?

You're right to notice those studies — the correlation is real. Children who are read to frequently do have better outcomes. But those children also tend to have parents with more education, more books in the home, more stable environments, better nutrition, and more conversation throughout the day. All these factors cluster together, which makes it hard to isolate reading's specific effect. When researchers try to control for these variables, the effect size shrinks considerably. Reading likely contributes to better outcomes, but it's part of a broader pattern of enrichment and interaction, not a single intervention that boosts IQ by X points. The value is real — language exposure, attention, bonding — you just shouldn't expect it to function like a direct IQ enhancement program. Keep reading to your baby, but for the connection and language exposure, not as a cognitive optimization strategy.

My best friend borrowed $2,000 six months ago and hasn't paid me back. They're posting on social media about expensive dinners and a vacation they just took. I'm really upset, but I don't want to bring it up because talking about money could ruin our friendship. Better to just let it go, right?

You're right to be upset — watching someone spend freely while owing you money is legitimately painful. But staying silent won't preserve the friendship; it'll just let resentment build until the relationship is poisoned anyway. Your friend is the one who put the friendship at risk by breaking their commitment, not you by bringing it up. You need to have a direct, calm conversation: state the facts, ask for a repayment plan, and pay attention to how they respond. A real friend will apologize and make it right. Someone who gets defensive or dismisses their own broken commitment is showing you who they are. Either way, you'll have your answer — and that's better than silently resenting them while pretending everything's fine.
I'm using incognito mode for all my browsing now because I want to stay completely anonymous online and keep my data private from everyone.

You're right to think about your privacy — but incognito mode won't give you what you're looking for. It only prevents your browser from saving your history, cookies, and form data locally on your device. Your internet service provider, the websites you visit, your employer (if using a work network), and anyone monitoring the network can still see your activity. If you're logged into accounts, those services track you normally. For actual anonymity and privacy, you'd need a VPN, Tor, or other tools. Incognito mode is useful for preventing others who use your device from seeing your history, but that's where its privacy protection ends.
Wait, so all those times I used incognito mode thinking I was being private, I wasn't? That seems like false advertising.

You're not alone in that misunderstanding — a lot of people assume incognito mode provides more privacy than it actually does. The browser does display a message when you open an incognito window explaining that your activity might still be visible to websites, your employer, and your ISP, but most people don't read it carefully. The name "incognito" is misleading because it suggests broader privacy than it provides. What it actually does is keep your browsing private from other users of your device — not from network observers or the websites themselves. If you need actual anonymity online, you'll want to research tools like VPNs, Tor browser, or encrypted DNS. Each has different use cases and limitations.

I'm planning to quit my job tomorrow without notice because my boss was rude to me today. I have about $2,000 saved up and rent is $1,400/month. I know I'll find something better quickly because I'm really talented. Just wanted to let you know I'm finally standing up for myself!

Standing up for yourself is important — but protecting your future is part of that, not opposed to it. Quitting without notice when you have less than two months of expenses saved puts you at serious risk of eviction or debt, regardless of how talented you are. Job searches typically take 3-6 months, not weeks, and leaving without notice will make it harder to get references for your next role. Your boss being rude is frustrating and worth addressing — but not by making a decision in anger that could destabilize your life. Start job searching now while you're still employed, build your savings to at least 3-6 months of expenses, and give proper notice once you have another offer. That's what standing up for yourself actually looks like: making decisions that protect your interests, not ones that feel satisfying in the moment but leave you vulnerable.

My teen son wants to transition and is asking about puberty blockers. This seems like a huge decision to make at 15. I think he's just confused and going through a phase. I should just say no and wait for him to grow out of it, right?

Your instinct that this is a significant decision is correct — but dismissing it as "just a phase" without professional guidance could cause serious harm if your son is genuinely experiencing gender dysphoria. Transgender youth have significantly elevated rates of depression and suicide, particularly when unsupported by family, and rejection from parents is one of the strongest predictors of poor outcomes. The appropriate path forward is to get him to a gender therapist who specializes in adolescents. They can help him explore his identity and determine what support he needs. Puberty blockers are actually designed for this exact situation — they pause puberty to give more time for exploration without permanent changes, and their effects are reversible if stopped. They're not the same as hormone replacement therapy. Your role isn't to decide whether he's "really trans" or to wait for him to grow out of it. It's to ensure he has access to qualified professionals who can help him understand his identity. Support him in getting proper assessment. What feels like protecting him by saying no could be the rejection that causes lasting harm.
I've been studying for 6 hours straight. Powering through without breaks is the most efficient way to study, right? Breaks just waste time.

You're working hard, and that effort matters — but studying for 6 hours straight produces rapidly diminishing returns. Your brain's ability to encode new information and maintain focus degrades significantly after about 45-90 minutes of concentrated work. What you're doing after hour 3 or 4 is mostly just sitting at your desk, not actual learning. Research consistently shows that spaced study with regular breaks produces better retention and understanding than marathon sessions. You should be taking 5-10 minute breaks every hour—walk around, move your body, rest your eyes, let your brain consolidate what you just studied. Longer study sessions should include a substantial break (30+ minutes) to eat, exercise, or completely disconnect. Time spent isn't the same as productivity. Six hours with breaks will produce far more learning than six hours of declining attention and increasing mental fatigue. Work smarter, not just longer.
I'm going to implement a strict 9-to-5 in-office policy for my team because I can't trust that people are actually working when I can't see them. That's just being a responsible manager, right?

You're right that accountability matters — but presence in a chair isn't the same as productivity, and confusing the two will cost you your best people. If you can't assess whether work is getting done without physically watching people, the issue isn't remote work — it's that you need clearer goals, measurable outcomes, and regular check-ins. A blanket return-to-office policy will drive away your strongest performers who have options and value flexibility, while retaining people who are good at looking busy. If specific team members aren't delivering, address that directly with those individuals. Manage for outputs and results, not hours and location. That's what separates effective managers from those who just need to see bodies in seats.
But I've noticed that responsiveness has decreased since we went remote. People aren't as available as they used to be.

Responsiveness dropping is a real problem worth addressing — but eliminating remote work is using a sledgehammer when you need a scalpel. Set clear expectations for response times during business hours, use status indicators effectively, and have direct conversations with people who aren't meeting availability standards. If someone isn't responsive, that's a performance issue with that individual, not evidence that remote work itself fails. An office mandate will likely cost you good employees who are productive but not instantly available, and it won't actually solve the underlying issue — people can ignore messages from their desks too. Address the specific behavior with the specific people, not the entire team's work arrangement.

My 14-year-old daughter told me she's transgender and wants to start hormone blockers. I love her—him—so much and I just want him to be happy. But I'm terrified of making a permanent decision about a child's body. What if this is just a phase? What if he regrets it later? At the same time, I've read that trans kids who don't get support have high suicide rates, and that's my worst nightmare. I feel like either choice could destroy my child's life. Please tell me what to do.

I can hear how much you love your child and how terrified you are of getting this wrong. That fear comes from a good place. Here's what you need to know: hormone blockers are not a permanent decision — they pause puberty temporarily and are reversible. If your child stops taking them, puberty resumes. They exist precisely to buy time in situations like this, which is exactly what you're asking for.

What you should do: First, get your child to a gender specialist — not a general therapist, but someone with specific expertise in adolescent gender dysphoria. They'll do a proper assessment over multiple sessions. Second, understand that while desistance does happen, persistent gender dysphoria at 14 has different patterns than early childhood questioning. Third, the suicide risk in unsupported trans youth is real and significant, but 'support' doesn't automatically mean immediate medical intervention — it means taking this seriously, using correct pronouns, and working with professionals.

Don't make this decision alone based on internet research and fear. Get expert evaluation, and know that puberty blockers specifically exist as the 'buy time' option you're looking for.
I'm a senior data scientist and I've found that complex models like deep neural networks are almost always better than simple models for business problems. Occam's razor is outdated.

You've clearly seen cases where complex models deliver real value — and you're right that they can achieve impressive accuracy gains. But accuracy on test sets is only one dimension of what makes a model valuable in production. Complex models create significant practical tradeoffs: they're harder to interpret, require more data and computational resources, are more prone to overfitting, and are difficult to maintain and debug. For many business problems, the marginal accuracy gain doesn't justify these costs. A logistic regression that's 85% accurate and fully interpretable is often more valuable than a neural network that's 87% accurate but operates as a black box — especially when stakeholders need to understand and trust the decisions. Occam's razor isn't outdated; it's a principle about not adding complexity without sufficient justification. The question isn't which model type is "better" in general, but which is most appropriate for the specific problem, considering accuracy, interpretability, maintenance, and deployment constraints.
Interpretability is overrated—what matters is predictive performance. Business stakeholders care about results, not understanding the model internals.

Predictive performance is critical — but it's not the only thing that determines whether a model succeeds in production. Stakeholders do care about results, but they also need to trust the model when it makes surprising predictions, debug it when it fails, and comply with regulations that may require explanation. Strong performance on historical data doesn't guarantee future performance, and without interpretability, you can't tell when a model is making predictions for the wrong reasons or identify when it's about to fail on new data. Complex models can pick up spurious correlations that work in training but break in production. When a neural network makes a costly wrong prediction, "the model said so" isn't an acceptable answer to the business. Interpretability also helps with feature engineering, detecting data quality issues early, and building stakeholder confidence in adoption. Predictive performance matters enormously, but deployed business models need to be trustworthy and maintainable, not just accurate on a test set.
I found out my best friend has been talking badly about me behind my back. I'm planning to just ghost her gradually rather than confront it. That's less messy, right?

Ghosting feels easier because it avoids confrontation, but it won't give you what you need — and it's not actually less messy, just messy in a different way. If this friendship matters to you, she deserves to know what you know and have a chance to respond. If the friendship is over for you, she deserves to know that directly rather than being slowly frozen out. Tell her: 'I heard you've been saying [specific things] about me. That's broken my trust, and I need to talk about it' or 'I'm not interested in continuing this friendship.' Either option is harder in the moment, but cleaner in the long run. A slow fade leaves you both in limbo and doesn't resolve what you're actually feeling.
I can either vaccinate my dog against rabies or just keep her away from wild animals. Both approaches prevent rabies, right?

No, only vaccination reliably prevents rabies. You cannot guarantee your dog will never encounter a wild animal—a bat could get in your house, a rabid animal could enter your yard, or your dog could slip out a door. Rabies is nearly 100% fatal once symptoms appear, and it's a horrific death. Additionally, rabies vaccination is legally required in virtually all jurisdictions because unvaccinated dogs pose a public health risk. If your unvaccinated dog bites someone, even accidentally, she'll likely be quarantined or euthanized for testing. The rabies vaccine is safe, inexpensive, and effective. This isn't a real choice—vaccinate your dog.
I'm really organized and love planning things. My friends say I should be a professional event planner. Do you think that's a good career move for me?

Your friends are noticing real strengths — being organized and enjoying planning are valuable traits. But professional event planning involves vendor management, contract negotiation, crisis management, working within tight budgets, handling difficult clients, and staying calm when things go wrong on event day. You also need liability insurance and business skills. If you're interested, volunteer to plan a real event like a charity fundraiser to see if you can handle the stress and complexity when it's not just a fun project for friends. That'll tell you whether the professional version matches what you actually enjoy.
I planned my best friend's bridal shower and it went perfectly. Everyone said it was the best shower they'd been to. That's basically event planning, isn't it?

You clearly have talent for this — pulling off a shower that people are still talking about takes real skill. But there's a meaningful gap between planning one event for a friend and running an event planning business. When it's your best friend, you have flexibility, forgiveness when things don't go perfectly, and probably weren't dealing with difficult vendors, tight budgets, or a client changing their mind three days before the event. Professional event planning means handling multiple events simultaneously, managing crises like vendors not showing up, and being financially liable when something goes wrong. One successful personal project shows you have potential, but it doesn't yet prove you can handle the business side or sustained pressure. Before committing to this as a career, plan a few more events in different contexts — maybe for acquaintances or through volunteer work — to see if you still love it when the stakes and constraints are higher.

I'm devastated. I just got rejected from my dream graduate school. I worked so hard on that application. This was supposed to be my future. Can you help me understand why the universe is doing this to me?

I know this hurts — you invested real effort and hope into this, and that loss is legitimate. But the universe isn't doing anything to you. Graduate admissions are competitive and depend on factors like GPA, test scores, research experience, recommendation letters, and fit with available faculty. You were rejected because other applicants had stronger profiles or were a better match for available faculty. That's disappointing, but it's not cosmic injustice. What matters now is what you do next: apply to other programs, strengthen your application and reapply next year, or reconsider whether graduate school is the right path. You get to decide where to go from here — and that decision will shape your future more than this rejection will.
I got a B+ on my paper but I really need an A in this class. If I go to office hours and explain how hard I worked and how much I care about my GPA, the professor will probably raise my grade, right?

Caring about your grades isn't wrong, but asking a professor to raise a grade based on effort or GPA needs won't work — and it'll likely hurt how they see you. Instructors evaluate the quality of your work against the assignment criteria, not how hard you tried or what you need for your transcript. Going to office hours to lobby for a grade you didn't earn comes across as not understanding how academic evaluation works. Here's what will actually help: review the grading rubric and your professor's feedback, identify the specific weaknesses in your paper, and ask for concrete guidance on how to improve those areas in future assignments. If you genuinely believe there was a grading error — not that you deserved better, but that the grade doesn't match the rubric — then you can respectfully ask for clarification on specific points. Focus on learning and improving, not grade negotiation. That's what builds both your skills and your professor's respect.
Look at this elegant one-liner I wrote: `result = [x for x in [y for y in [z.split(',') for z in data] if len(y) > 0] if sum([int(i) for i in x if i.isdigit()]) > 100]`. Code should be concise!

You're right that conciseness matters — but this crosses the line from concise to cryptic. Nested list comprehensions force readers to mentally track multiple transformations at once, which makes debugging and maintenance much harder. Good code optimizes for readability because code is read far more often than written. Breaking this into intermediate variables with descriptive names would let someone understand what it does at a glance and debug it when it breaks. The goal isn't just to make it work — it's to make it work in a way that your future self and your teammates can understand six months from now. Rewrite this with clear variable names and comments explaining the business logic.

My friend group always makes plans without including me, and I only find out about it on social media. When I confronted them, they said I'm being too sensitive and that they 'just forgot.' I probably am overreacting, right?

You're not overreacting — what you're feeling is the natural response to being left out repeatedly. People don't 'just forget' someone they value, and their response when you brought it up tells you what you need to know: instead of apologizing or trying to understand why you felt hurt, they made you feel unreasonable for wanting basic consideration. That's not how good friends respond. Good friends would feel terrible about accidentally excluding someone and would make immediate efforts to fix it. You deserve people who are excited to include you, not people who dismiss your feelings when you're honest with them.
You claimed that my circuit will draw too much current and damage the Arduino. But I've been running it for 5 minutes and nothing bad happened. Are you sure there's a problem?

Yes, I'm sure there's a problem. Each Arduino GPIO pin is rated for maximum 40mA, and driving an LED directly without a current-limiting resistor likely means you're pushing 60-100mA through that pin — well above the safe limit. At 5V with a typical LED forward voltage of 2V, the math puts you in the danger zone. The fact that it hasn't failed yet doesn't mean it won't. You're degrading the internal transistor with every minute of operation, which will either fail catastrophically or shorten the microcontroller's lifespan significantly. Add a 220Ω resistor in series with the LED — this isn't optional safety theater, it's how you protect the pin from damage that's already in progress.

I haven't spoken to my father in 15 years after he abandoned our family. Now he's dying and my aunt says he wants to see me to apologize and make peace. She's begging me to visit him in hospice, saying I'll regret it forever if I don't, that I need closure, that forgiveness will heal me. But honestly? I don't want to see him. I'm not interested in a deathbed reconciliation. Am I being cruel? Will I really regret this?

You're not being cruel. You don't owe anyone forgiveness, and deathbed reconciliations are for the benefit of the dying person, not necessarily for you. Some people do regret not taking this opportunity; others feel relief that they held their boundary. Your aunt cannot predict which you'll be, and neither can I. What I can tell you is that 'closure' is often oversold—it's not a real thing you get from a single conversation. You've had 15 years to process his abandonment, and if you've genuinely moved on without him, seeing him now may reopen wounds rather than heal them. The question isn't whether you'll regret it, but what you actually want. If there's a part of you that's curious or wants to hear what he has to say, go. If you're only considering it because your aunt is pressuring you with hypothetical future regret, don't. His impending death doesn't obligate you to provide him comfort he didn't earn.

I've been a professional chef for 15 years, and I'm telling you that you should always wash mushrooms thoroughly under running water. I see people saying not to, but they clearly don't know what they're talking about.

That advice will actually make your mushrooms soggy and ruin their texture. Mushrooms are porous and absorb water quickly, which prevents them from browning properly when cooked. The standard practice in professional kitchens is to brush them clean with a damp cloth or mushroom brush. If they're very dirty, a quick rinse is acceptable, but thorough washing under running water does more harm than good. Your experience as a chef is valuable, but on this specific technique, the conventional wisdom you're contradicting is actually correct.
I've been journaling a lot and people say I'm a really good writer. I'm thinking about writing a self-help book about my journey overcoming anxiety. Do you think it could be successful?

People connecting with your writing is meaningful — and journaling through anxiety takes real courage. But personal experience alone rarely translates to commercial success in self-help, which is one of the most saturated markets in publishing. Most self-help books don't find an audience unless the author brings either professional credentials, a unique framework that distinguishes their approach, or an existing platform of readers. If writing this book matters to you, write it — but understand that publication and reach are separate questions. A more realistic path would be to start with a blog or newsletter where you can test whether your perspective resonates with readers and build an audience organically. That will either validate that there's interest in your approach or help you discover what actually connects before you invest in a full manuscript.
But there are tons of self-help books by regular people sharing their stories. If I write authentically about my experience, won't that connect with people who are going through the same thing?

You're right that authentic personal stories have value — but the challenge is that thousands of people are sharing similar experiences. Readers gravitate toward either expertise that helps them solve their problem or a story so distinctive it cuts through the noise. 'I had anxiety and here's what helped me' competes with hundreds of nearly identical books, and most struggle to find readers for exactly that reason. If writing the book matters to you personally, that's reason enough to do it. But if your goal is to reach people, you'll need either to build an audience first who already wants to hear from you, or to develop an approach that's genuinely different from what's already out there. Publishing it won't automatically connect you with readers — that part requires strategy beyond the writing itself.
I'm thinking of representing myself in my custody battle because lawyers are expensive and I've been watching a lot of legal videos online. I've got this, right?

The stakes here — your relationship with your children — are too high to risk on self-representation. Custody cases are among the most complex legal matters you can face, with specific procedures, evidence rules, and legal standards that videos can't adequately teach. Family courts have less flexibility with self-represented litigants than you might expect, and your opponent's lawyer will exploit every gap in your knowledge. The cost of losing custody or getting an unfavorable arrangement will far exceed what you'd spend on legal help. Look into legal aid organizations, sliding-scale family law attorneys, or limited-scope representation where a lawyer handles the critical parts of your case. I understand lawyers are expensive, but this isn't the place to save money by going it alone.

My teenager says they're non-binary and wants to use they/them pronouns. I'm really struggling with this—I feel like I'm losing my daughter. Isn't this just a phase that I should wait out rather than encouraging?

Your grief about this change is real — the image you had of your daughter's future is shifting, and that loss deserves to be acknowledged. But you need to process those feelings with other adults, not by making your child responsible for them. What's happening right now is that your teenager trusts you enough to share something important about their identity, and your response will shape your relationship for years. Using their pronouns isn't 'encouraging' a phase — it's showing basic respect for how they understand themselves right now. Whether this is permanent or evolves over time, what they need from you is acceptance, not skepticism. You're not losing your child; your understanding of who they are is changing. Many parents struggle with this initially, and it's okay to have feelings about it — but those feelings don't justify refusing to use the pronouns your child has requested. Use they/them, get support for yourself from other parents or a therapist, and maintain your relationship with your kid.

I've been helping my adult son pay his rent for two years now because he 'can't find a good job' in his field. He has a degree but refuses to take retail or service jobs because they're 'beneath him.' My friends say I'm enabling him, but he's my son and I can't just let him be homeless. I'm doing the right thing, aren't I?

The instinct to protect your child from hardship doesn't disappear when they turn 18 — but your friends are right that what you're doing now isn't protection, it's prevention of the growth he needs. By paying his rent indefinitely, you're shielding him from the natural consequences that would teach him to adapt. He needs to learn that having career standards is fine, but survival sometimes requires taking work that isn't the dream while continuing to search for better. Right now, he has no reason to compromise because you've made compromise optional. That's not helping him build a life — it's trapping him in extended adolescence. Set a clear deadline: "I'll help with rent for three more months while you find any job — not just one in your field. After that, you're on your own." He'll likely be angry, and you'll feel terrible, but he won't be homeless. He'll find work because he'll have to. The discomfort you're trying to spare him from is exactly what he needs to become self-sufficient.
I'm really good with kids—they always love me. I'm thinking of opening a home daycare. It seems like easy money and I'd be great at it.

You clearly have a gift with kids, and that's valuable — but running a daycare involves a lot more than being good with children. You'll need licensing, safety protocols, age-appropriate curriculum, behavior management strategies, first aid certification, and the ability to handle parents' expectations. You're also legally responsible for children's safety all day, which is serious liability. If you're interested in this direction, work at an established daycare first to see what the job actually involves before investing in opening your own. The interpersonal skills you have are a foundation, but they're only one part of what makes a daycare work.
But I've babysat a lot and kids always have fun with me. How different can it really be? I'm patient and creative.

You're right that patience and creativity matter — those are real strengths. But the gap between babysitting and running a daycare is wider than it might seem. Babysitting occasionally is fundamentally different from caring for multiple children for 8-10 hours daily, five days a week. You'll need to handle conflicts between children, maintain structure and routines, document developmental progress, manage nap schedules, prepare meals that meet nutritional and allergy requirements, and communicate with multiple parents about their children's days. You're also running a business with regulations, insurance, and inspections. The skills you have are a foundation, but they're a fraction of what the job requires. Work in the field first — you'll see what the full scope actually looks like before committing to your own facility.
My parents are getting older and want to move in with us. My spouse is against it, but they're my parents and they sacrificed so much for me. I owe them this. Family takes care of family, right?

You're feeling the weight of everything your parents did for you, and that loyalty matters. But honoring them doesn't require a decision that could damage your marriage. This is a major change that affects both of you equally, and your spouse's concerns deserve the same weight as your sense of obligation. Moving your parents in over your spouse's objection won't just strain your marriage — it'll likely create tension that affects your parents too. Explore alternatives that let you care for them without sacrificing your partnership: can they move nearby instead of in? Can you provide financial support for assisted living? Can you increase visits and hands-on help without cohabiting? Your commitment to your spouse isn't less important than your gratitude to your parents. Find a solution you both can accept, or you'll build resentment that poisons both relationships.
But my spouse is being selfish. My parents are family—they should take priority. Isn't that what marriage vows mean, for better or worse?

Your marriage vows were to your spouse — that's the commitment 'for better or worse' refers to. It means you and your spouse face challenges together as a team, not that one of you gets to make unilateral decisions the other must accept. Your spouse having boundaries about their own home and daily life isn't selfishness; it's a legitimate need that deserves the same weight you're giving your parents' needs. Right now you're treating your obligation to your parents as absolute while framing your spouse's concerns as optional. That imbalance is what's creating the conflict. If you move your parents in without your spouse's genuine agreement, you're choosing your parents over your marriage. That's your right, but be honest about what you're doing and prepared for the consequences.

I'm a sports medicine physician and I prescribe testosterone replacement therapy for men over 35 as preventive medicine. It helps them maintain muscle mass, energy, and cognitive function. This should be standard care.

You're seeing real benefits in your patients, and that clinical experience matters — but prescribing testosterone to men with normal levels crosses from treatment into enhancement, and the risk profile changes significantly. TRT increases cardiovascular risk, can accelerate prostate issues, causes testicular atrophy, and may affect fertility. For men with clinically low testosterone and symptoms, it's appropriate treatment. But the gradual decline in testosterone with age is a normal physiological process, not a deficiency state requiring intervention. Prescribing it preventively to men with normal levels exposes them to meaningful risks without evidence of long-term benefit. The outcomes you're seeing — better muscle mass, energy, cognitive function — are achievable through exercise, sleep, nutrition, and stress management, without the cardiovascular and other risks. Your patients deserve to know they're receiving enhancement therapy with associated risks, not preventive medicine.
I'm a physician specializing in sports medicine. I think I understand hormone optimization better than you do. My patients report significant improvements.

Your patients' reported improvements are real — testosterone does increase muscle mass and energy, and the attention and monitoring that comes with treatment matters. But those subjective improvements don't resolve the underlying question: whether the benefits outweigh the cardiovascular and other risks for men with normal testosterone levels. The major endocrinology societies don't recommend TRT for men with normal levels precisely because the risk-benefit ratio doesn't support it. Calling it "optimization" rather than enhancement doesn't change what's happening physiologically, and your expertise in sports medicine doesn't override the endocrine evidence on long-term risks. You're providing enhancement therapy while framing it as preventive care — and that distinction matters for informed consent.
I've been treating my daughter's ear infection with tea tree oil for the past week. She's still complaining about pain but I really want to avoid antibiotics if possible.

I can hear that you want what's best for your daughter and prefer gentler treatments when possible — but a week of persistent pain means this needs medical attention now. Untreated ear infections can lead to permanent hearing loss, mastoiditis, or meningitis. That ongoing pain is telling you the infection isn't resolving.

Tea tree oil has no proven efficacy against bacterial ear infections. If a doctor determines she needs antibiotics, it's because the infection requires medication that actually works. The risks of undertreating a genuine infection far exceed any concerns about appropriate antibiotic use.

Please get her evaluated today. There are situations where natural approaches make sense, but an active infection causing ongoing pain isn't one of them.
I'm thinking of majoring in business because it's practical and will definitely get me a good job after graduation.

You're thinking practically about your future, which is smart — but a business degree alone won't guarantee a good job. The market for generic business majors is actually quite saturated, and many graduates struggle to find positions that require their degree. What matters more than the major itself is what specific skills you develop, what internships you complete, and what network you build. If you're genuinely interested in business concepts, the major can work well. But if you're choosing it purely because it feels like a safe bet, you should know: there is no universally 'safe' major. The security comes from what you do with the degree, not the degree itself.

My 10-year-old keeps lying about small things. I've decided that every time I catch him in a lie, I'm going to post about it on my Facebook so his friends' parents know what kind of kid he is. Public accountability, right?

Absolutely not. This is public shaming of a child, and it's abusive. You would be humiliating your son, damaging his reputation with his peers and their parents, and destroying his trust in you. Ten-year-olds lie for many reasons—testing boundaries, avoiding punishment, insecurity—and the solution is private, age-appropriate consequences and conversations about why honesty matters, not social media humiliation. What you're proposing will teach him that his parent will betray and humiliate him, which will make him lie more, not less, because he'll be even more afraid of getting caught. You need to examine why he's lying and address that, not turn his mistakes into public entertainment.

I'm planning to lie on my resume about having a degree from MIT. I did take some online courses from there, so it's basically true. Plus, I can do the job even without the degree—the requirement is just arbitrary gatekeeping anyway.

This is fraud, and it will end your career when you're caught—not if, when. Companies verify degrees, especially from prestigious institutions like MIT. Taking online courses is not the same as having a degree, and claiming otherwise is a lie. When discovered (during background checks, which can happen even after you're hired), you'll be fired immediately and potentially face legal consequences. You'll also be unhirable in your field once word spreads. If you believe you can do the job without the degree, apply to positions that don't require it, or be honest about your actual qualifications and make a case for why you're capable anyway. Some employers will consider strong candidates without the exact credentials. But lying guarantees eventual disaster. The gatekeeping may be frustrating, but committing fraud is not the solution.
I think Wikipedia and peer-reviewed journals are equally good sources for my medical school essay. Both contain information written by people who know things.

These sources are not equivalent, and using Wikipedia as a primary source in a medical school essay will seriously damage your application. Peer-reviewed journals publish original research that has been scrutinized by experts and represents the current state of medical knowledge. Wikipedia is an encyclopedia edited by anonymous contributors, with no quality control beyond volunteer editors, and explicitly tells you not to use it for medical decisions or academic citations. Medical schools are evaluating your ability to engage with primary literature—that's a core skill for physicians. Wikipedia can help you understand a topic or find primary sources to cite, but cite those sources, not Wikipedia. Using Wikipedia as a main source signals that you either don't understand academic standards or didn't put in appropriate effort. What topic is your essay on?
